explain.say: Standing on two legs is tricky because the body's weight must stay above the small area of the feet. If the centre of mass leans past the edge, the robot starts to tip.

faq.q: How does a robot know it is falling?
faq.a: An inertial measurement unit, with gyroscopes and accelerometers, senses tilting and turning hundreds of times a second. If the lean grows, the controller reacts straight away.
asks: What sensors help a robot balance?

faq.q: What is the centre of mass of a robot?
faq.a: It is the point where its weight acts as if it were all concentrated. A standing robot stays upright while that point stays above the area its feet cover, called the support area.
asks: Why does a robot tip over?

faq.q: What happens if you push a walking robot?
faq.a: A good walking robot feels the push, shifts its weight with its ankles and hips, and if needed takes a quick step to catch itself, much like a person stumbling.
asks: Can robots recover from a push?

faq.q: Why do four-legged robots balance more easily?
faq.a: With more legs on the ground they have a wider support area, so the centre of mass is less likely to fall outside it. Even so, running robot dogs still use fast balance control.
asks: Why are robot dogs so stable?

faq.q: Why is walking called controlled falling?
faq.a: Each step starts by letting the body tip forward, then a leg swings out to catch it. Repeating this smoothly moves you forward, for people and robots alike.

facts: Honda's ASIMO, first shown in 2000, was one of the first humanoid robots to walk smoothly on two legs.
Humanoid robots use inertial measurement units, combining gyroscopes and accelerometers, to sense tilt.

quiz.why: Moving a foot under the leaning body puts the support area back beneath the centre of mass.
